analysis.one_liner: Strips states of the power to require food safety warnings stricter than federal rules.
analysis.headline: With 119 cosponsors from both parties, the bill died in a House subcommittee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal food law to bar states and cities from enforcing any food safety warning or disclosure requirement unless it is identical to federal rules. States could still petition the federal Health Secretary for an exemption or to push a federal standard, and could act on their own only for an imminent health hazard. Several narrower state rules — freshness dates, organic labels, unit pricing, restaurant sanitation advisories — would be carved out.
analysis.who_benefits: Large food and beverage manufacturers and distributors. They would deal with one national set of warning and labeling rules instead of a patchwork of state requirements — most notably stronger state warning laws like California's — and would avoid putting extra warning labels on products sold nationwide.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it illegal for a state or locality to enforce any food warning requirement — covering labels, posters, notices, and advertising — unless the requirement is identical to one prescribed under federal food law [S2][S3].
It also extends preemption to state requirements on a long list of specific federal food provisions, so a state rule that differs from federal law in those areas could not stand [S3].
For companies selling food nationwide, this eliminates the cost and legal risk of meeting different warning rules in different states.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers, who would lose state-mandated warnings about food hazards whenever federal rules are weaker or absent, and state governments, which would lose their authority to warn their own residents about food safety risks.

drawbacks.text: A single national standard does have value: companies shipping food across state lines would no longer face 50 different warning regimes, and federal rules are set through a science-based process [S2][S3].

The honest cost: if the federal government sets no warning for a hazard, no state could require one either. States could only act alone for an 'imminent hazard' likely to cause serious health consequences or death, and even then must petition the federal Secretary and can act only after the Secretary has not moved — so the federal government becomes the gatekeeper for nearly all food warnings [S3].

The bill does preserve some state authority — freshness dating, organic and religious labeling, unit pricing, restaurant sanitation advisories, and state product liability law are expressly untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: National uniformity is a real convenience for food companies and removes genuinely inconsistent state rules. But the trade is a federal ceiling: consumers in states that chose stricter warnings would lose them, and replacing a state warning with a federal petition process that can take months puts decisions about local food hazards in Washington's hands. The bill is drafted to serve industry's need for one rulebook more than consumers' need for the strictest available warning.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health and Environment Subcommittee in June 1999, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Burr introduced the bill on June 10, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it stayed; the record shows no markup, no floor action, and no vote for the rest of the 106th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 119 cosponsors — 89 Republicans, 29 Democrats, and 1 independent — a level of support that never translated into legislative action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and the consumers who rely on stronger state food warning laws are better off, since nothing changed; the food industry did not get the national preemption it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and consumers kept their warning laws

for.name: Rep. Richard Burr
for.role: U.S. Representative, North Carolina; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a large bipartisan cosponsor group behind it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health and Environment Subcommittee and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 89 Republicans, 29 Democrats, and 1 independent signed on — and no recorded vote ever separated the parties, because the bill never left committee.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and processors
industries.note: The bill would replace stricter state warning requirements with a single federal ceiling, sparing manufacturers extra warning labels and multi-state compliance costs. The gain comes directly out of consumers' access to warnings about food hazards.

A uniform national rule covers advertising and in-store notices, so retailers would avoid state-by-state warning signage and disclosure rules. The saving comes from not having to tell shoppers about hazards some states wanted disclosed.
States would lose the power to warn residents about food hazards beyond federal rules, keeping only narrow carve-outs and a petition process that requires federal sign-off.
